title: The Caliph al-Hakim and the Merchant
summary: The Fatimid Caliph Al-Hakim bi-Amr Allah, who ruled Egypt from Cairo, was famous for his nightly tours through the city, riding a grey donkey through the bazaars in simple attir...
keywords: the caliph al-hakim and the merchant
full_text:
The Fatimid Caliph Al-Hakim bi-Amr Allah, who ruled Egypt from Cairo, was famous for his nightly tours through the city, riding a grey donkey through the bazaars in simple attire to inspect market weights and prices with relentless vigilance.

During a year of severe drought, when the Nile failed to flood its banks, the price of grain skyrocketed. Greedy merchants hoarded wheat in their warehouses, creating an artificial famine and selling flour at exorbitant prices to the starving citizens.

One evening, Al-Hakim stopped his donkey before the shop of an honest grain merchant named Abu Ali. While all the surrounding shops were demanding ten dinars for a measure of grain, Abu Ali continued to sell his wheat at the normal, fair price of two dinars, measuring each scoop with scrupulous accuracy.

Al-Hakim, disguised as a poor laborer, stepped forward and asked: 'O merchant, why do you not double your price like your neighbors? You could amass a fortune in gold before the week ends.'

Abu Ali looked at the customer with clear, honest eyes and answered: 'Brother, I purchased this wheat before the drought at fair cost. Shall I profit from the tears of hungry children and the misery of my neighbors? A single dirham gained by honest measure carries a blessing, while mountains of gold amassed through extortion are nothing but hot coals in the hand.'

Al-Hakim was deeply moved. The next morning, the Caliph summoned the merchants of Cairo to his palace.

Before the assembled assembly, the Caliph threw off his disguise, severely punished the hoarders, and appointed Abu Ali as the Grand Inspector of the Markets of Egypt, decreeing that only those who fear the heavens and love their fellow men are worthy to oversee the bread of the people.
moral: Honest commerce that refuses to exploit scarcity brings honor and royal protection.
